growth_story.headline: Sierra Leone's income per person shrank through war, surged with peace, crashed with Ebola and iron ore, and is back near its 1982 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Sierra Leone peaked in 1982, then slid as diamond revenues dwindled and the state weakened. From 1990 to 2001 it shrank 3.4 percent a year as the civil war that began in 1991 brought brutal fighting and mass displacement, and it fell 17.5 percent in 1992 alone. Peace in 2002 brought a rebound of 19.4 percent that year, and from 2002 to 2013 income per person grew 5.1 percent a year, led by farming and, from 2011, two large iron ore mines. That run ended abruptly when Ebola struck and iron ore prices collapsed, shutting the mines: income per person fell 10.0 percent in 2014 and 6.6 percent in 2015, so the era from 2014 to 2025 averages only 0.2 percent a year. Since then the recovery has been steady but modest, at 1.9 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, through a fall of 3.5 percent in 2020 and a bout of very high inflation that peaked in 2023. Income per person is now 3.3 percent below its 1982 peak and about where it first was in 1974.

threads.title: Civil war and its end
threads.text: Years of economic decline and grievance ended in a civil war in 1991 that lasted more than a decade, fuelled by diamonds. Peace in 2002 opened the longest stretch of rising income per person since independence.

threads.title: Ebola and the iron ore bust
threads.text: In 2014 and 2015 the Ebola epidemic and a slump in iron ore prices hit at the same time. Both iron ore mines stopped producing, and growth in the rest of the economy nearly stalled.

threads.text: Prices rose very fast, with inflation peaking in late 2023. IMF directors link low growth and high inflation to outside shocks combined with weak policy and governance. Tight policy brought inflation down sharply by late 2025.

threads.text: The economy still relies on a narrow set of exports and heavy imports of food, fuel and fertilizer, which leaves it exposed to price shocks. Most jobs are informal, and nearly half of workers farm at low productivity.

since_last_year.text: Sierra Leone ended 2025 with stronger growth and low inflation, but the war in the Middle East has since raised fuel, food and shipping costs. Inflation climbed again through mid-2026. The World Bank expects growth to slow in 2026, and the IMF notes spillovers from the war.

citations.quote: Growth is projected to slow to 4.0 percent in 2026 as higher input and transport costs weaken agricultural, industry, and trade-related services.

growth_story.tension: The IMF and World Bank describe solid GDP growth in 2022, 2023 and 2025, but income per person grew 3.0, 3.4 and 2.5 percent in those years, because the population keeps growing. More than two decades after peace, and after an era of 5.1 percent growth a year, income per person is still 3.3 percent below its 1982 peak.
